titre: Lake Nyos, 1986: The Gas Came From the Lake Bottom
accroche: In Cameroon, in August 1986, about 1,700 people die. According to the measurements, the killer is CO2 stored in the lake's deep water, not an eruption.
contenu_vulgarise:
On August 21, 1986, around 9:30 p.m., rumblings lasting 15 to 20 seconds bring residents near Lake Nyos, in northwestern Cameroon, out of their homes. One witness sees a white cloud rise from the water and a wave swell. Many smell rotten eggs or gunpowder, feel a sensation of heat, then lose consciousness. Survivors wake between 6 and 36 hours later, often with their oil lamps out and their relatives dead. About 1,700 people and 3,000 cattle perished, up to 10 kilometers from the lake. The vegetation is practically intact. The outside world learns nothing until August 24, when two pilots from a Swiss mission fly over the area.

## Volcano or Lake?

Nyos sits in a recent volcanic crater: the reflex is to talk about an eruption. The investigating team, on site from August 27, tested this hypothesis, and it failed. An injection of magma or hot gas would have warmed the water: at Soufrière on Saint Vincent, a crater lake had reached 82°C. At Nyos, the measurements of September 4 and 5 show cool water at almost the same temperature from top to bottom; in twelve days, the lake could have cooled by only 0.5°C, so a strong injection of heat would have left traces. A sediment sample from the bottom contains no fresh volcanic constituent.

## Gas Stored at the Bottom of the Lake

According to Kling and his coauthors, this is a matter of lake chemistry. CO2 of magmatic origin dissolved in the groundwater that feeds Nyos. The deep water, richer in dissolved substances, stayed beneath the surface water without mixing, and the gas built up in the bottom waters of a lake whose floor reaches 208 meters. At saturation, the lake could hold 1.5 km³ of it; Kling and his coauthors estimate that 1.2 km³ were released, which would have lowered the level by about 110 cm, in agreement with the observations of the pilots and villagers. Denser than air, the cloud filled the basin to about 100 meters above the rim, then flowed down into the valleys.

The victims died of asphyxiation. At nonlethal doses, CO2 acts as an anesthetic and can make people smell sulfur compounds that aren't there, which explains the rotten-egg odor. According to Kling and his coauthors, the survivors' skin lesions come mostly from the position held during unconsciousness, with a few burns from contact with a heat source and illnesses that predated August 21; they find no evidence of chemical burns.

## What the Story Shifts

The trigger remains unknown: if the water was nearly saturated, any small disturbance could have been enough, according to the authors. The authors recorded no significant seismic shaking at the Kumba station, 220 kilometers away, and note a landslide scar that looks fresh but that they cannot date. A lake can therefore be deadly without any eruption: its chemistry can be measured and monitored. A similar episode at Lake Monoun in 1984 had killed 37 people. In 2016, after some fifteen years of artificial degassing through pipes that siphon off the deep water, the lake is considered relatively safe, and the dispute over the cause has given way to agreement. How many other deep lakes carry dissolved gas beneath water that does not mix?

repere.texte: Kling and his coauthors (1987) estimate that at saturation Lake Nyos could hold 1.5 km³ of CO2 and that about 1.2 km³ were released on August 21, 1986, which would have lowered the lake level by about 110 cm, in agreement with the observations of the pilots and villagers.
repere.source: Kling et al., “The 1986 Lake Nyos Gas Disaster in Cameroon, West Africa,” Science, 236, 1987

carte.punch: Lake Nyos, 1986: no direct volcanic activity. The gas lay dissolved in the deep water.
carte.idee: According to Kling and his coauthors, the lake was cool, with no heat input: CO2 of magmatic origin had built up in the bottom water. Kling and his coauthors estimate 1.2 km³ of gas released, or about a 110 cm drop in level, for about 1,700 deaths.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Overview of the disaster and of the lake's degassing.

quiz.question: Which observation, made about two weeks after the Nyos disaster, contradicts the hypothesis of a direct volcanic eruption?
choix: The lake had kept scalding water in all its layers for several days
No trace of gas was found in the lake's deep water
All the affected villages were built on the slopes of an active volcano
Cool water, at roughly the same temperature from top to bottom
quiz.explication: An injection of magma or hot gas would have warmed the lake, as at Soufrière on Saint Vincent, where the temperature rose to 82°C. At Nyos, the measurements of September 4 and 5, 1986 show cool, nearly isothermal water, and the lake could have cooled by only 0.5°C in twelve days. The other answers are wrong: the gas was indeed found dissolved in the deep water, and nothing indicates that the villages were on an active volcano.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the card, what explains the rotten-egg smell noticed by many survivors?
choix: CO2, at nonlethal doses, can make people smell sulfur compounds that aren't there
The gas really did contain large amounts of hydrogen sulfide
The smell came from overturned oil lamps burning
The gas had carried decomposing algae up from the lake bottom
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says CO2, at nonlethal doses, acts as an anesthetic and can make people smell sulfur compounds that aren't there; it is neither real hydrogen sulfide nor any other cause mentioned in the card.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the outside world learn of the Lake Nyos disaster?
choix: A radio call from surviving villagers as early as August 22
A weather satellite detects the cloud on the evening of August 21
Two pilots from a Swiss mission fly over the area on August 24
International seismographs record the event live
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says the outside world learns nothing until August 24, when two pilots from a Swiss mission fly over the area; the other three options do not appear in the card.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which other lake does the card cite as having experienced a comparable deadly degassing two years earlier?
choix: Lake Monoun, in 1984, with 37 deaths
Lake Kivu, in 1990, with no victims
Lake Chad, in 1986, with no gas at all
Lake Victoria, in 1988, dried up completely
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text mentions a similar episode at Lake Monoun in 1984, which had killed 37 people; none of the other three lakes appears in the card.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Kling and his coauthors' estimates, what happened to the lake's level after the gas was released?
choix: It rose by about 110 cm, the gas having pushed water toward the surface
It dropped by about 110 cm, matching the volume of gas released
It stayed perfectly stable; no change was measured
It dropped by several meters, nearly emptying the lake
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kling and his coauthors estimate that the 1.2 km³ of gas released would have lowered the lake level by about 110 cm, in agreement with the observations of the pilots and villagers, not a rise or a stable level.
